name: יחדשהו לכסלו — Y'chad'sheihu for Kislev
note: This Kislev setting uses the Maoz Tzur tune, related to a sixteenth-century German chorale and possibly an earlier folk melody; the date is approximate.

name: אדון עולם — Adon Olam
note: Rossi's choral Adon Olam was issued among the Hebrew sacred works of Ha-shirim Asher li-Shlomo. The marker records the documented 1623 Venice edition rather than a precise composition date.

name: ברכו — Barechu
note: This polyphonic Barechu belongs to Rossi's Ha-shirim Asher li-Shlomo, printed in Venice in 1622–23. The marker records publication, not an undocumented first performance.

name: אלוהים השיבנו — Elohim Hashivenu
note: This choral setting from Psalm 80 appears in Ha-shirim Asher li-Shlomo. The year and place refer to the securely dated 1623 Venice printing; its precise composition date is unknown.

name: השכיבנו — Hashkivenu
note: Rossi's five-voice Hashkivenu is part of Ha-shirim Asher li-Shlomo, an early printed collection of polyphonic Hebrew liturgical music. The marker records its Venice publication in 1623.

name: קדיש — Kaddish
note: Rossi's polyphonic Kaddish was printed in Venice in Ha-shirim Asher li-Shlomo. The year marks the securely documented printed source, prepared in 1622–23, rather than a known composition or premiere date.

name: שיר המעלות אשרי כל ירא ה׳ — Psalm 128
note: Rossi set Psalm 128, Shir Hama'alot Ashrei Kol Yerei Adonai, for multiple voices in Ha-shirim Asher li-Shlomo. The entry uses its definite 1623 printed-source date.

name: על נהרות בבל — Psalm 137
note: Al Naharot Bavel, Rossi's Psalm 137, was printed in Ha-shirim Asher li-Shlomo. The date refers to that definite 1623 Venice edition, not a securely known composition date.

name: הללויה הללי נפשי — Psalm 146
note: Rossi's four-voice Halleluya Haleli Nafshi appears in Ha-shirim Asher li-Shlomo. Its 1623 Venice marker represents the documented printed source rather than an exact composition or performance date.

name: למנצח על הגתית — Psalm 8
note: Lamnatzeach Al Hagittit, Rossi's polyphonic Psalm 8, was printed in Ha-shirim Asher li-Shlomo. Its placement at 1623 records the dated Venice edition and does not assert a known premiere.

name: מזמור שיר ליום השבת — Psalm 92
note: Rossi's eight-voice Mizmor Shir L'Yom HaShabbat was published with his Hebrew synagogue works. The map uses the definite 1623 Venice edition date rather than an inferred composition date.

name: אז ישיר משה — Az Yashir Moshe
note: An old Ashkenazi cantillation for the Song at the Sea, sharing motifs with other victory-associated liturgical formulae; the map date is only a broad historical anchor.

name: מעוז צור — Venetian Ashkenazi melody
note: An old Italian-Ashkenazi melody for Maoz Tzur was written down and reused by Benedetto Marcello in his Estro poetico-armonico during the 1720s. The marker represents this early surviving notation, not the unknown date when the Jewish melody first arose.
composer: Traditional; transcribed and adapted by Benedetto Marcello

name: אלי ציון — Eli Tzion
note: The ubiquitous Tisha B'Av melody is documented by 1743, though its composer and route into Jewish practice are unknown. Idelsohn identified related European religious and folk melodies; Frankfurt is used only as a Central European anchor.

name: אין כאלוהינו — Handel melody
note: On Shabbat Chanukah some communities sing Ein Keloheinu to See, the Conquering Hero Comes from Handel's Judas Maccabaeus, premiered in London in 1747. The Jewish textual adaptation is later and is not dated by this marker.
composer: George Frideric Handel; later Jewish contrafactum

name: אדיר הוא — Adir Hu
note: A traditional Ashkenazi melody for the concluding Passover Seder hymn Adir Hu; the map point is a broad historical anchor.

name: קואנדו אל ריי נמרוד — Cuando el Rey Nimrod
note: This Ladino narrative of Abraham's birth circulated widely in Sephardi communities; its date and Istanbul marker are broad historical anchors.

name: אל מלך יושב — El Melech Yosheiv
note: An old penitential melody introducing the Thirteen Attributes during Selichot; its precise origin and date are unknown.

name: למי אבכה — L'mi Evkeh
note: A Sephardi elegy for Tisha B'Av evening whose melody circulated orally; Amsterdam and the date provide only a broad historical anchor.

name: קה אכסוף — Kah Echsof (Karlin)
note: The hymn was written by R' Aharon the Great of Karlin and became a defining Karlin-Stolin Shabbat melody. The date marks its late-eighteenth-century Hasidic setting approximately, not a documented premiere.
composer: Traditional Karlin; words by R' Aharon the Great of Karlin

name: ניגון רבי מיכל מזלוטשוב — Nigun of R' Michel of Zlotchov
note: A devotional nigun traditionally associated with R' Yechiel Michel of Zlotchov. Its placement falls within his lifetime; no exact composition year is known.
composer: Traditionally attributed to R' Yechiel Michel of Zlotchov

name: שלוש תנועות — Shalosh Tenuot
note: This three-part Chabad nigun links musical phrases associated in tradition with the Baal Shem Tov, the Maggid of Mezritch and the Alter Rebbe. The date and location are a historical anchor for the transmission rather than a precise composition claim.

name: יגדל לפסח — Yigdal for Pesach
note: One of three characteristic festival Yigdal melodies associated with Duke's Place in the late eighteenth century, and possibly older North German or Bohemian practice.

name: יגדל לשבועות — Yigdal for Shavuot
note: The solemn Shavuot member of the three festival Yigdal melodies associated with Duke's Place in the late eighteenth century.

name: יגדל לסוכות — Yigdal for Sukkot
note: The Sukkot member of the characteristic festival Yigdal melodies associated with Duke's Place in the late eighteenth century.

name: ארבע בבות — Daled Bavos
note: The four-section contemplative nigun of the Alter Rebbe is among the central melodies of Chabad. Its year is an approximate late-eighteenth-century anchor.

name: אדיר במלוכה — Adir Bimlucha
note: A traditional Passover melody for Adir Bimlucha whose precise origin and date remain undocumented.

name: אדון עולם לימים נוראים — Adon Olam for High Holy Days
note: A solemn traditional Adon Olam variant for the High Holy Days; its oral transmission does not permit an exact date.
aliases: אדון עולם לימים נוראים — Adon Olam for High Holy Days

name: אבינו מלכנו — Avinu Malkeinu (Alter Rebbe)
note: One of the melodies traditionally counted among the ten compositions of the Alter Rebbe. The date is approximate.

name: בני היכלא — Bnei Heichala (Chabad)
note: The Chabad melody for the Arizal's Shalosh Seudot hymn is traditionally included among the Alter Rebbe's melodies. The year is approximate.
composer: Traditionally attributed to R' Shneur Zalman of Liadi
performance: Avraham Fried, Motty Steinmetz, Akiva and Benaia Barabi, male vocals

name: בצאת ישראל — B'tzeit Yisrael
note: A traditional British Hallel melody strongly preserved in the United Kingdom but little known elsewhere; the date is approximate.

name: דרכך — Dark'cha
note: A traditional synagogue melody for Dark'cha whose composer, date, and exact place of origin are not known.

name: אין כמוך לימים נוראים — Ein Kamocha for High Holy Days
note: A traditional High Holy Day variant of Ein Kamocha, preserved through synagogue custom rather than a documented composition.
aliases: אין כמוך לימים נוראים — Ein Kamocha for High Holy Days

name: המבדיל — Hamavdil
note: A traditional melody for Hamavdil at the close of Shabbat; its oral history does not support an exact date or single place of origin.

name: הורם מה שיאמרו — Horeim
note: A sombre traditional melody for the Rosh Hashanah Musaf supplication before the verses of Kingship, Remembrance and Shofar. Its origin is unknown, so the date and Frankfurt-area location are broad tradition anchors only.

name: א־לי אתה — Keili Atah (Alter Rebbe)
note: A setting of verses from Hallel, preserved as one of the Alter Rebbe's ten melodies. The date is approximate.
performance: Rabbi Menachem Feldman and The Great Synagogue Choir, male vocal

name: כי הנה כחומר — Ki Hinei Kachomer
note: An old melody for the Kol Nidrei-night piyut that remains prevalent in Britain and is echoed during Ne'ilah. Its authorship and date are unknown; the marker is only a broad Central European tradition anchor.

name: מי כמוכה לסוכות — Mi Chamocha for Sukkot
note: The Lulawschütteln tune functions both while shaking the four species in Hallel and as a broader Sukkot musical motif; its date is approximate.

name: ניע זשוריצי כלאָפּצי — Nye Zhuritsi Chloptzi
note: An early Chabad song in Russian/Yiddish encouraging Hasidim not to worry but to trust in God. Its map date is approximate.

name: אודך — Od'cha
note: A joyful major-key Hallel melody preserved particularly in British synagogues and associated with the Duke's Place tradition.

name: אמנם כן — Omnam Kein
note: A responsive melody for the Yom Kippur selichah by Yom Tov of Joigny. Stuart's notes describe the tune as traditional and probably German; no composer or secure date is known.

name: שמע קולנו — Sh'ma Koleinu
note: A traditional Ashkenazi melody for the central Selichot petition Sh'ma Koleinu; its precise age and provenance are unknown.

name: סאָל אַ קאָקאָש מאַר — Szól a Kakas Már
note: The Kaliver tradition associates this Hungarian song with ר׳ יצחק אייזיק מקאליב; the date is a broad early-nineteenth-century anchor.

name: צור משלו — Tzur Mishelo
note: A buoyant traditional melody for the widely shared Shabbat zemirah. Claims of a German drinking-song source are speculative, and neither composer nor place of origin is known; the marker is only a broad Ashkenazi circulation anchor.

name: ויהי בנסוע — Vay'hi Binsoa
note: An old Duke's Place Torah-processional melody whose final line survives widely in Commonwealth synagogue practice.

name: יחדשהו לאב — Y'chad'sheihu for Av
note: A traditional seasonal melody for blessing the month of Av; neither a composer nor an exact date is securely documented.

name: יחדשהו לאלול — Y'chad'sheihu for Elul
note: A traditional melody used to give Birkat HaChodesh the penitential colour of Elul; the origin is oral and the map point approximate.

name: יחדשהו לסיון — Y'chad'sheihu for Sivan
note: A traditional seasonal melody for blessing the month of Sivan and anticipating Shavuot; its exact origin is unknown.

name: יחדשהו לתמוז — Y'chad'sheihu for Tammuz
note: A seasonal Birkat HaChodesh melody associated with the penitential character of Tammuz; its precise origin is unknown, so the date and location are broad historical anchors.

name: ניגון ברדיטשוב — Berditchever Nigun
note: A traditional devotional melody associated with the court of R' Levi Yitzchak of Berdychiv. The year is an approximate late-life anchor for the Berditchever Rav.

name: הבו לה׳ — Havu Ladonai
note: Bolaffi's setting of Psalm 29 became his best-known work and spread through Sephardi and Ashkenazi communities. The approximate date places it during his leadership of synagogue music in Livorno.

name: מארש נפוליון — Napoleon's March (Chabad)
note: Chabad tradition associates the adoption of this march with the Franco-Russian War of 1812 and the Alter Rebbe's spiritual opposition to Napoleon.
composer: European military tune adopted into Chabad tradition

name: הודו לה׳ לשבועות — Hodu Ladonai for Shavuot
note: The opening theme is documented as a Shavuot Hodu melody dating at least to the early nineteenth century; the recording combines it with a complementary melody.

name: אשרי — Ashrei
note: Sulzer's setting of Ashrei reflects the influential Viennese synagogue style disseminated through his Schir Zion collections; the year is approximate.

name: אין כמוך — Ein Kamocha
note: Sulzer's setting became one of the most widespread melodies for the Torah-service text Ein Kamocha; the year is approximate.

name: אין כאלוהינו — Ein Keloheinu
note: One of several settings Saqui included in his Songs of Israel, a major collection of British synagogue music; the date is approximate.

name: עץ חיים היא — Eitz Chayim Hi
note: Sulzer's setting of Eitz Chayim Hi became part of the international repertoire shaped by his Viennese Schir Zion collections; the date is approximate.
aliases: עץ חיים היא — Eitz Chayim Hi

name: הללויה — Halleluyah
note: Italian cantor-composer Michele Bolaffi's setting of Halleluyah is anchored approximately to his nineteenth-century Livorno period.

name: ניגון חסידי הצמח צדק — Nigun of the Chasidim of the Tzemach Tzedek
note: A Chabad nigun preserved from the generation of the Tzemach Tzedek. The midpoint of his leadership is used as an approximate map date.
aliases: Nigun of Chassidim of Tzemach Tzedek

name: ויהי בנסוע — Vay'hi Binsoa
note: Sulzer's setting of the Torah-processional verses represents the influential Viennese synagogue sound disseminated through Schir Zion.

name: ויאמר ה׳ סלחתי — Vayomer Adonai
note: Sulzer set the verse repeated near the opening of Kol Nidrei, connecting Moses's plea after the spies' sin with the congregation's request for forgiveness.

name: אין כאלוהינו — Ein Keloheinu
note: Freudenthal's melody was printed in Hirsch Goldberg's Gesänge für Synagogen in 1841 and became the dominant modern setting. Claims that it originated as a drinking song are unsupported.

name: הודו על ארץ ושמים — Hodo Al Eretz
note: Sulzer's waltz-like setting of the end of Psalm 148 became particularly popular in North American congregations. The approximate date places it within his mid-nineteenth-century Vienna repertory.

name: שמע ישראל — Sulzer and traditional melody
note: The familiar Torah-service sequence combines material associated with Sulzer's Ki Mitzion and an older congregational response. The approximate Vienna date marks its appearance in the mid-nineteenth-century Sulzer tradition, not a single act of composition.

name: אנא ה׳ הושיעה נא — Sukkot melody
note: The Lulawschütteln theme appears in nineteenth-century scores by Sulzer, Lewandowski, Baer and others and is used while shaking the four species. Its earlier origin is unknown; Vienna and 1850 are documentation anchors.

name: עץ חיים היא — Eitz Chayim Hi
note: Naumbourg, chief cantor in mid-nineteenth-century Paris, set this passage with the principal theme unusually placed in the bass and dedicated the piece to Gioachino Rossini.

name: קדיש לליל שבת — Kaddish for Shabbat Evening
note: A traditional Friday-night half-Kaddish melody with identifiable British, American, and other regional variants; the London date is only a representative anchor.

name: לכה דודי לבין המצרים — L'cha Dodi for Ben HaMetzarim
note: Naumbourg's setting reflects the custom of changing the L'cha Dodi melody during the Three Weeks; the date is an approximate Paris-career anchor.
aliases: לכה דודי לבין המצרים — L'cha Dodi for Ben HaMetzarim

name: לכה דודי לספירה — L'cha Dodi for S'firah
note: A traditional minor-mode melody used in some communities during the Omer; its exact origin and date are unknown.

name: מי כמכה — Shavuot melody
note: An old pan-Ashkenazi Shavuot theme, originally associated with Akdamut and documented in nineteenth-century synagogue scores. Its origin is earlier and unknown; Frankfurt and 1850 are only a Central European documentation anchor.

name: ניגון הכנה — Nigun Hachana of R' Hillel Paritcher
note: A profound preparatory nigun associated with R' Hillel Paritcher and sung before a Chasidic discourse. The date is approximate.
composer: Traditionally attributed to R' Hillel Paritcher

name: ניגון ל״ו — Nigun Lamed-Vav of R' Hillel Paritcher
note: A contemplative melody numbered 36 in the Chabad Sefer HaNigunim and associated with R' Hillel Paritcher. The date is approximate.

name: שאו שערים — S'u Sh'arim
note: Naumbourg's setting of the Torah-processional text S'u Sh'arim belongs to his influential Paris repertoire; the date is approximate.

name: שלום עליכם — Yekkish melody
note: A characteristically Western Ashkenazi melody with an irregular metre, older than Israel Goldfarb's familiar setting. Its precise age and author are unknown; Frankfurt and 1850 are representative rather than documentary.

name: טומבאַלאַלײַקע — Tumbalalaika
note: A traditional Yiddish riddle and courtship song transmitted orally across Eastern Europe; the map date and place are broad anchors.

name: ואני תפילתי — Va'ani T'filati
note: Naumbourg's unison choral setting accompanies the festival petition recited before taking out the Torah; the year is approximate.

name: לכה דודי לבין המצרים — L'cha Dodi for Ben HaMetzarim
note: Japhet's setting preserves the historical practice of using a distinctive L'cha Dodi melody during the Three Weeks; the year is an approximate publication-period anchor.

name: השיבנו — Hashiveinu
note: Emanuel Aguilar printed this melody in 1857 for B'motzaei Yom M'nucha; it later became familiar with the words Hashiveinu.

name: שאמיל — Shamil
note: Chabad tradition interprets the captive Imam Shamil's yearning melody as a parable for the soul's longing. The year marks Shamil's 1859 surrender and is a historical anchor, not a proven date of adaptation.
composer: Caucasian folk melody adopted into Chabad tradition

name: אדון עולם — Adon Olam
note: Simon Waley's major-minor setting was adopted by London's Spanish and Portuguese and Ashkenazi congregations. The date is an approximate marker for Waley's work with the West London Synagogue.

name: ויהי בנסוע — Vay'hi Binsoa
note: Emile Jonas's setting of the Torah-processional text belongs to the nineteenth-century French consistorial synagogue repertoire; the year is approximate.

name: ברוך הבא — Baruch Haba
note: Mombach's ceremonial wedding setting was notably sung for the 1865 marriage of Ferdinand de Rothschild and Evelina de Rothschild. Its grand choral style reflects the formal Victorian synagogue wedding service.

name: ובשופר גדול — Uvashofar Gadol
note: This High Holy Day setting, especially its K'vakarat section, entered the shared synagogue repertoire. It is attributed to Odesa cantor Wolf Shestapol, whose unpublished music survives only in fragmentary collections; Stuart Izon's version is a reconstruction from several sources. The map date is an approximate point in Shestapol's Odesa career.

name: אתה נותן יד — Ata Noten Yad
note: This N'ilah setting is one of the rare surviving written compositions associated with the influential Odesa cantor and teacher Betzalel Shulsinger. The date is an approximate midpoint in his nineteenth-century Odesa career.

name: הללו — Hal'lu
note: Mombach's Hal'lu setting is anchored to his long service in London's Great Synagogue; the date is approximate.

name: הבו לה׳ — Havu Ladonai
note: Mombach's Havu Ladonai is anchored approximately to his work at London's Great Synagogue.

name: היום הרת עולם — Hayom Harat Olam
note: Mombach's setting serves the solemn Rosh Hashanah declaration Hayom Harat Olam; the year is an approximate London-career anchor.

name: הודו לה׳ — Hodu Ladonai
note: Mombach's Hodu Ladonai is anchored approximately to his long service at London's Great Synagogue.

name: הודו לה׳ — Dukes Place Sukkot melody
note: A festive Hodu melody preserved in the Dukes Place tradition and documented as reaching back at least into the nineteenth century. The map year is deliberately approximate because no individual composer or first performance is known.

name: כי לקח טוב — Ki Lekach Tov
note: A lesser-known major-key Mombach setting for the Torah-service text Ki Lekach Tov; the year is an approximate London-career anchor.

name: לה׳ הארץ — Ladonai Ha'aretz
note: The second of four Mombach settings of Psalm 24 is an elaborate choral work now often associated with the High Holy Days. The approximate year places it in Mombach's mature service at London's Great Synagogue.

name: לה׳ הארץ — Ladonai Ha'aretz
note: Mombach's regal processional setting of Psalm 24 became one of the best-known melodies for returning the Torah on weekday festivals. Its exact date is unknown; the marker represents his mature Great Synagogue period.

name: לך ה׳ — L'cha Adonai
note: Mombach's Torah-processional setting shares thematic material with his festival Sh'ma and became established in British synagogue practice.

name: לכה דודי לספירה — L'cha Dodi for S'firah
note: Blumenthal's distinctive L'cha Dodi for the Omer belongs to the nineteenth-century Eastern European synagogue repertoire; the year is approximate.
aliases: לכה דודי לספירה — L'cha Dodi for S'firah

name: לכה דודי לספירה — L'cha Dodi for S'firah
note: Mombach's distinctive Omer-period L'cha Dodi reflects the historical practice of varying synagogue melodies by season.

name: לכתחילה אריבער — L'chatchila Ariber
note: A favorite melody of the Rebbe Maharash, linked with his maxim to go over an obstacle from the outset. The date is approximate within his leadership.
composer: Attributed to R' Shmuel Schneersohn, the Rebbe Maharash

name: מה אשיב לפסח — Ma Ashiv for Pesach
note: Mombach's Pesach setting opens with an emphatic declaration, incorporates the festival leitmotif, and uses musical word-painting.

name: מעוז צור — Mombach variant
note: Mombach modified the second line of the familiar German-derived Maoz Tzur melody so that it modulates to the dominant. His variant spread widely through British congregations; the marker dates the London adaptation approximately.
composer: Traditional German melody; modified by Julius Mombach

name: מזמור שיר ליום השבת — Mizmor Shir
note: Mombach's choral setting of Psalm 92 became the traditional British Ashkenazi melody for Shabbat Mincha, although his score places it in Kabbalat Shabbat. The exact composition year is unknown; the marker represents his mature London period.

name: שמע ישראל — Sh'ma Yisrael
note: Mombach's festival setting of Sh'ma became traditional in many British synagogues and is often followed by his related L'cha Adonai.

name: ונתנה תוקף — Un'tane Tokef
note: Nissan Blumenthal's setting of Un'tane Tokef comes from the nineteenth-century Eastern European cantorial tradition; the date is approximate.

name: וכך היה מונה — V'chach Haya Moneh
note: One of Mombach's two responsive settings for the High Priest's counting during the Yom Kippur Avodah. The exact date is undocumented, so the marker places it approximately within Mombach's mature work at London's Great Synagogue.

name: ושמרו — V'sham'ru
note: Lewandowski's harmonised setting was originally major-sounding, although later congregational transmission often recast the melody in minor. The marker represents his Berlin Kabbalat Shabbat repertory.

name: יציב פתגם — Y'tziv Pitgam
note: An older melody for the Aramaic Shavuot poem was reshaped by Julius Mombach in the nineteenth century to fit its three-line units. The marker records that London adaptation, not the unknown origin of the tune.

name: ה׳ רועי — Adonai Ro'i
note: This Hebrew setting uses the Scottish hymn tune commonly called Crimond, associated with Jessie Seymour Irvine and first published in the nineteenth century; 1872 is a publication-era anchor.

name: אדון עולם — Adon Olam
note: Eliezer Gerovitch printed this universally familiar melody as an Alte Weise, or old tune, indicating that it was already traditional in Russia during his lifetime.

name: אהבת עולם — Ahavat Olam
note: Marcus Hast's antiphonal choral setting for the High Holy Days moves between a triumphant major opening, a slower minor middle section and the traditional festival evening motif. Its exact date is unknown; the marker places it approximately during Hast's tenure at London's Great Synagogue.

name: ביום ההוא — Bayom Hahu
note: A setting by Haim Wasserzug, cantor of London's North London Synagogue, for the concluding declaration of Aleinu; the date is approximate.

name: עץ חיים היא — Eitz Chayim Hi
note: Nissan Blumenthal's enduring setting became so widespread that it is often described as traditional. The map date is an approximate late-nineteenth-century Odesa anchor, not a documented first performance.

name: אשא עיני — Esa Einai
note: Verrinder, Anglican organist of the West London Synagogue, composed this classic setting of Psalm 121 in the late nineteenth century. It later became strongly associated with remembrance services.

name: ראָזשינקעס מיט מאַנדלען — Rozhinkes mit Mandlen
note: Goldfaden wrote this celebrated Yiddish lullaby for his operetta Shulamis around 1880.
source: YouTube performance and standard work chronology

name: ועל חטאים — V'al Chataim
note: Lewandowski's choral setting of V'al Chataim forms part of the late-nineteenth-century Berlin High Holy Day repertoire; the year is approximate.

name: ועל ידי עבדיך — V'al Y'dei Avadecha
note: Lewandowski's setting exemplifies the monumental late-nineteenth-century Berlin synagogue style; the year is approximate.
aliases: ועל ידי עבדיך — V'al Y'dei Avadecha

name: וזאת התורה — V'zot Hatorah
note: Lewandowski's setting of the declaration made while raising the Torah exemplifies the late-nineteenth-century Berlin synagogue style.

name: זכרנו לחיים — Zochreinu
note: Haim Wasserzug's plaintive late-nineteenth-century setting became a traditional melody in Nusach Anglia. Its precise composition year is not known, so the marker uses an approximate date during Wasserzug's London cantorial career.

name: כל נדרי — Kol Nidrei, Op. 47
note: Max Bruch composed this concert work for cello and orchestra from Jewish liturgical melodies, including Kol Nidrei, in 1880–81.
source: YouTube performance and standard work chronology

name: לך ה׳ הגדולה — L'cha Adonai
note: One of Lewandowski's settings for the Torah procession, using the verse from I Chronicles 29. The approximate year represents his mature Berlin publication period.

name: ניגון פולטבה — Poltava Nigun
note: The melody is associated with R' Yaakov Mordechai Bezpalov's prolonged prayer in Poltava; the historical account specifically anchors it in 1882.

name: שמע ישראל — Sh'ma Yisrael
note: Lewandowski's setting of Sh'ma Yisrael belongs to the monumental Berlin synagogue repertory he published in the later nineteenth century. The approximate year reflects the publication era of Kol Rinnah u-Tefillah rather than a documented composition day.

name: ויהי בנסוע לחגים — Vay'hi Binsoa for Festivals
note: Lewandowski wrote these stately themes for Ata Horeita on Simchat Torah; they later became associated with taking out the Torah on festivals.

name: וכך היה אומר — V'chach Haya Omer
note: Lewandowski's responsive setting accompanies the climactic confession in the Yom Kippur Avodah, when the congregation answers the High Priest's declaration. The marker uses his mature Berlin publication era because a precise composition or premiere date is not documented here.

name: והגן בעדנו — V'hagein Ba'adeinu

note: A Carlebach setting of Psalm 102 expressing love and hope for Zion. Jerusalem in the late 1960s is used as an approximate contextual anchor.

name: ירושלים של זהב — Jerusalem of Gold
note: Naomi Shemer wrote both words and melody for the 1967 Israel Song Festival. The song was first performed shortly before the Six-Day War and soon acquired exceptional national resonance.

name: אדון עולם — Adon Olam
note: A liturgical adaptation using music associated with Andrew Lloyd Webber; the map year is an approximate early-career anchor rather than a documented date for the adaptation.

name: ברכי נפשי — Borchi Nafshi
note: A lyrical Carlebach setting of the opening words of Psalm 104. The historical placement is approximate.

name: ממקומך — Mimkomcha (Carlebach)
note: Carlebach's setting of Mimkomcha from the Shabbat Kedushah. The date and Jerusalem marker are approximate.

name: ישראל בטח בה׳ — Yisrael Betach BaShem
note: Carlebach's setting of the Hallel verse calling Israel to trust in God. The date is approximate.

name: ממקומך — Mim'kom'cha
note: Ben Zion Shenker composed this melody on a flight to Israel in 1968 after a conversation with Knesset member Yitzchak Meir Levin.

name: על אלה — Al Eileh
note: Stephen Levey's setting of the Tisha B'Av lament Al Eileh is anchored approximately to his London compositional career.

name: כל העולם כולו גשר צר מאוד — Gesher Tzar Me'od
note: Baruch Chait's famous setting of the teaching attributed to R' Nachman of Breslov. The date and New York marker are approximate career anchors.

note: Carlebach's setting of the blessing for Jerusalem from Birkat Hamazon. The year is approximate.

note: A widely sung Carlebach melody expressing hope for the rebuilding of the Temple. The date is approximate.

name: ממקומך — Mim'kom'cha
note: Stephen Levey's setting of the Shabbat Kedushah passage expresses its aspiration for restored divine sovereignty in Jerusalem; the date is approximate.

name: אנעים זמירות — Anim Zemirot
note: A London-school choral setting of Anim Zemirot associated with Yigal Calek. The date is approximate within the choir's early recording period.

name: יום שבתון — Yom Shabbaton
note: Yigal Calek's modern setting of the Sabbath hymn Yom Shabbaton is anchored approximately to his London years.

name: למען אחי ורעי — L'ma'an Achai
note: Aviezer Wolfson's setting of the verse from Psalm 122 was recorded by Yigal Calek's London School of Jewish Song in 1976. The precise composition date may be earlier, so this marker uses the securely described first-recording year.

name: מי שברך לחיילי צה״ל — Mi Sheberach for Tzahal
note: The melody was originally written for Eretz Tzvi, commemorating the 1976 Entebbe rescue, and was later adopted for the prayer for Israel's soldiers.

name: הללויה — Halleluyah
note: Kobi Oshrat composed the melody for the song Halleluyah, performed by Milk and Honey and winner of the 1979 Eurovision Song Contest in Jerusalem. Stuart Izon's arrangement applies the melody to the Hebrew text of Psalm 150 rather than the original song lyrics.

name: ברכות הבדלה — Birchot Havdalah
note: Debbie Friedman's modern Havdalah melody became ubiquitous across Jewish denominations; the date is an approximate compositional-era anchor.

name: מלך עליון — Melech Elyon
note: Geoffrey Shisler's modern setting of the High Holy Day poem Melech Elyon is placed approximately in his British cantorial career.

name: ואני תפילתי — Va'ani T'filati
note: Geoffrey Shisler's modern setting of Va'ani T'filati is placed approximately in his British cantorial career.

name: נער הייתי — Na'ar Hayiti
note: Peshy Stulberger composed this Birkat Hamazon melody, later recorded and popularised by Abie Rotenberg; the date is approximate.

name: אחינו כל בית ישראל — Acheinu
note: Rotenberg's widely adopted prayer-song for Jews in distress, released through the Lev V'Nefesh repertoire. The year is approximate.

name: בצאת ישראל — B'tzeit Yisrael
note: Sue Straus-Mariner composed this lyrical antiphonal setting of Psalm 114 and was associated with Belsize Square Synagogue. No reliable composition year has been located, so 1990 is only a provisional map anchor within her modern London period and should not be read as a documented date.

name: לכה דודי — L'cha Dodi

name: אוחילה לאל — Ochila La'el

name: שמרו שבתותי — Shimru Shabtotai
note: Eliezer Diamond composed a family melody for this less familiar Shabbat-day zemer; the date and New York location are approximate.

name: ושמרו — V'sham'ru
note: Mark Raphael's modern setting of V'sham'ru is represented at an approximate late-twentieth-century British compositional point.

name: משיח — Moshiach
note: Mona Rosenblum's major early-1990s Orthodox popular composition on longing for the Messiah. The Jerusalem location is an approximate professional anchor.

name: ידיד נפש — Y'did Nefesh
note: Abie Rotenberg composed this lesser-known setting of Y'did Nefesh during the 1990s. The midpoint of that decade and Toronto are used as an approximate career anchor.
